statement: In healthy adults tested the morning after an evening of heavy drinking, with blood alcohol back near zero, the morning after compared with a day without alcohol or with placebo is associated with poorer short-term and long-term memory, sustained attention and reaction speed: pooled standardized differences of about half to two-thirds of a standard deviation (short-term memory g = 0.64, 95% CI 0.15 to 1.13, five studies; long-term memory 0.59, 0.01 to 1.17, four studies; sustained attention 0.47, 0.07 to 0.87, four studies; reaction speed 0.66, 0.31 to 1.00, five studies), with no pooled effect on divided attention, mixed results for working memory, and no clear effect in single studies of problem solving, management simulations or examination scores (Gunn et al., 2018). Each estimate pools a few small studies with moderate to high heterogeneity (I2 36% to 84%); sleep was rarely controlled, nobody could be blinded, naturalistic studies with more drinking found impairment more often than laboratory studies, and the review did not separate people who felt hungover from those who did not, so the finding describes the morning after heavy drinking rather than hangover symptoms as such. A later simulator study found slower responses on a divided-attention task during a drive the morning after a night of social drinking, including in drivers with no alcohol left in their breath (Alford et al., 2020). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: The morning after heavy drinking, even with no alcohol left in the blood, people in studies remembered less, kept their attention less well and reacted more slowly than on a day without alcohol, by a medium amount on average. The studies were small, often did not control sleep, and could not hide from people whether they had been drinking, so how big the effect really is remains uncertain.
population: Healthy adults, mostly young (students and cadets in several studies), tested the morning after an evening of heavy drinking in 19 controlled laboratory and naturalistic studies from 1970 to 2016 summarized in one systematic review; and 52 young drivers in one later simulator study
exposure: An evening of heavy drinking, given in the laboratory or chosen by participants in naturalistic studies, with the hangover confirmed by questionnaire and blood alcohol near zero at testing (study amounts are on the study cards)
comparator: The same people on a morning after no alcohol or placebo, or a separate group without a hangover
outcome: Next-morning performance on memory, attention, reaction-time, working-memory and executive tasks
magnitude: Hedges' g, positive meaning worse after drinking: short-term memory 0.64 (95% CI 0.15 to 1.13; 5 studies; I2 73%); long-term memory 0.59 (0.01 to 1.17; 4 studies; I2 84%); sustained attention 0.47 (0.07 to 0.87; 4 studies; I2 50%); reaction speed 0.66 (0.31 to 1.00; 5 studies; I2 36%); divided attention, 4 studies, no detectable effect (no estimate reported); working memory and executive tasks not pooled. Later simulator study: divided-attention response time slower the morning after drinking, d = 0.55 in 52 drivers and 0.69 in the 26 with zero breath alcohol (authors' effect sizes, no intervals).

evidence.page: PMC HTML, Results › Memory › Short-term memory
evidence.locator: Results › Memory › Short-term memory, 1st paragraph; Figure 4 legend
evidence.extracted: Seven studies measured short-term memory: three reported impairment (one in women only) and four did not; pooled over five studies, Hedges' g = 0.64 (95% CI 0.15 to 1.13), I2 = 73%, P = 0.01, worse after heavy drinking.

evidence.page: PMC HTML, Results › Memory › Long-term memory
evidence.locator: Results › Memory › Long-term memory, 1st paragraph; Figure 5 legend
evidence.extracted: Four studies measured long-term memory: the three word-recall studies found impairment and the study in which material was learned while sober did not; pooled g = 0.59 (0.01 to 1.17), I2 = 84%, P = 0.05.

evidence.page: PMC HTML, Results › Attention › Sustained attention
evidence.locator: Results › Attention › Sustained attention, 1st paragraph; Figure 3 legend
evidence.extracted: Five studies measured sustained attention (three laboratory, two naturalistic): three reported impairment and two did not; pooled over four studies, g = 0.47 (0.07 to 0.87), I2 = 50%, P = 0.02.

evidence.page: PMC HTML, Results › Psychomotor performance › Speed
evidence.locator: Results › Psychomotor performance › Speed, 1st paragraph; Figure 6 legend; Discussion, 4th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Reaction time was slower in three naturalistic studies, and three laboratory studies found no evidence of slowing; pooled over five studies, g = 0.66 (0.31 to 1.00), I2 = 36%, P < 0.001. One of those laboratory studies could not be pooled for lack of information, which the authors say may inflate the estimate.

evidence.page: PMC HTML, Results › Attention › Divided attention; Results › Memory › Other memory; Results › 'Real-life' simulations
evidence.locator: Results › Attention › Divided attention, 1st paragraph; Results › Memory › Other memory, 1st paragraph; Results › 'Real-life' simulations, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Divided attention: only one of five studies (n = 5) found impairment, and the meta-analysis of four showed no evidence of an effect (no estimate given). Working memory was mixed (impairment on one of three tasks in one study). No clear effect on a ship power-plant problem, managerial simulations or examination scores.

The authors state that people in the hangover conditions may have had no symptoms, so the review examines next-day effects of heavy drinking rather than hangover as such; that naturalistic studies, with more alcohol, were more likely to find impairment; and that condition and task order were not always randomized, nicotine was not always controlled and the sleep allowed varied between studies.

evidence.locator: Table 1, Divided Attention › Mean Response Time row; Results › 3.1 Driving Performance, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: During a simulated commute, divided-attention response time was slower on the morning after a night of social drinking than after a night without alcohol: 3.5 (SD 1.8) against 2.4 (1.3) in all 52 drivers, d = 0.55 (ANOVA F(1,50) = 15.6, p < 0.0001), and 3.4 (1.6) against 2.3 (1.0) in the 26 with zero breath alcohol, d = 0.69.

risk_of_bias.note: The pooled memory and reaction-speed estimates rest mainly on naturalistic, non-randomized within-person comparisons; testing could not be blinded, task order was not always randomized, sleep was rarely controlled, and the review is of critically low confidence (model not stated, no assessment of blinding or confounding).

inconsistency.note: I2 of 50% to 84% for three of the four pooled domains; naturalistic studies tended to find impairment where laboratory studies did not, an explanation proposed but not tested.

indirectness.note: The claim is worded for the morning after heavy drinking in healthy adults, as studied; it does not claim effects of hangover symptoms as such.

imprecision.note: Four or five small studies per estimate; the long-term memory interval reaches down to 0.01, and divided attention has no estimate.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed; small positive studies dominate, and several null studies were excluded by the strict inclusion criteria or are not accounted for among the exclusions.

grade.reasoning: Started low because the pooled estimates for memory and reaction speed come mainly from naturalistic comparisons in which people chose their drinking nights; the randomized placebo-controlled laboratory studies within the review mostly found smaller or no effects. Downgraded for risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision and suspected publication bias, which leaves very low certainty; starting high for the laboratory studies would give the same result after these downgrades. Status replicated: impairment was found by at least two independent groups in each pooled domain (for example McKinney and Coyle, Grange and colleagues, Howland and Rohsenow), with null results mainly in small laboratory studies at lower amounts; the direction of every pooled estimate is the same. The later simulator study adds one consistent observation on response speed but used a different task from those pooled.
